title: Jollof One-Pot Rice
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: A three-stage build on a ready-made jollof sauce — and if the sauce isn't hot enough before the rice goes in, the rice soaks up cold water and goes soggy.
longDesc: This is jollof built from components: a jollof sauce and a dry spice mix made in advance, both published separately. The chicken simmers twenty minutes in half the spice mix, then bakes twenty to twenty-five minutes until crisp while the broth is reserved. The remaining onions are softened with the rest of the spice mix, chilli powder, curry powder and three hundred and fifty millilitres of sauce, and the broth goes back in. Washed rice is stirred in, the reserved sauce ladled over without stirring, and the pan covered with foil and a lid for fifteen to twenty minutes.
ingredients: 300 g basmati or long-grain white rice
6-8 bone-in chicken portions, thighs or drumsticks
1 scotch bonnet chilli, deseeded and diced
Olive or groundnut oil, for the first stage
Shito (GHA051) or green kpakpo shito salsa
equipment: Large heavy pan with a lid
steps: Sauté half the onions in oil, add the chicken with the garlic, thyme, bay leaf, guinea peppers, scotch bonnet and 1 tablespoon of the spice mix.
Cover with water and simmer 20 minutes, until tender.
Meanwhile heat the oven to 180 degrees and bake the chicken 20 to 25 minutes, until crisp. Reserve the broth.
Heat the 4 tablespoons of oil and sauté the remaining onions until soft.
Add the remaining spice mix, the chilli powder, the curry powder and 350 ml of the jollof sauce.
Wash the rice in three changes of cold water, until it runs clear.
Stir the rice into the sauce.
Ladle in the reserved sauce WITHOUT stirring.
Cover with foil and the lid and cook 15 to 20 minutes, until the liquid absorbs and the rice is tender.
chefTips: The warning is the most useful line in any jollof recipe: if the sauce isn't hot enough before adding the rice, the rice will soak up the cold water and become soggy. Everything must be at a simmer when the rice goes in.
Three changes of cold water until clear. More thorough than most recipes ask and it matters at this hydration.
Ladle the reserved sauce in WITHOUT stirring. That is what gives the top and bottom different characters rather than one uniform rice.
Foil AND the lid, which is the same trick as the Nigerian party-jollof method. It traps steam far better than a lid alone.
Three hundred and fifty millilitres of the five hundred goes in with the aromatics; the rest is ladled over at the end. Keep the split.
Simmer the chicken then CRISP it in the oven. Boiled-then-baked gives you cooked-through meat with a browned exterior.
Add water gradually if the rice dries out — her own note, and it is the recovery move if the ratio is off.
commonMistakes: Adding rice to a sauce that is not hot.
Stirring after the reserved sauce is ladled in.
Washing the rice once rather than three times.
All the sauce in at the start.
sources: Adapted from 'Jollof One-Pot Rice' by Zoe Adjonyoh, from Zoe's Ghana Kitchen (Octopus), published across three outlets. (1) octopusbooks.co.uk, 5 February 2021, BYLINE AS PRINTED 'By Hazel O'Brien' with the recipe credited to Adjonyoh — so the byline is the publisher's staff writer, not the author. (2) taste.co.za, 23 March 2021, credited to Zoe Adjonyoh. (3) oprah.com, NO BYLINE OR DATE printed, photography Nassim Rothacker. ALL THREE PAGES WERE FETCHED ONCE ONLY — SINGLE-PASS — although the core quantities agree across all three, which is a form of corroboration.

Ingredients exactly as printed in the Octopus version: 2 large onions, finely chopped; Olive oil or groundnut oil; 6–8 bone-in chicken portions (thighs or drumsticks); 2 garlic cloves, very finely chopped; 1 tablespoon thyme leaves; 1 large bay leaf; 5–6 guinea peppers, crushed; 1 Scotch Bonnet chilli, deseeded and diced; 2 tablespoons Jollof Dry Spice Mix; 1 teaspoon crushed sea salt; 4 tablespoons groundnut oil or sunflower oil; 1 teaspoon hot chilli powder; 1 teaspoon curry powder; 500ml Jollof Sauce; 300g basmati or long-grain white rice; Chopped parsley or coriander, to garnish; Shito or Green Kpakpo Shito Salsa, to serve. Yield as printed: 'Serves 6'.

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE THREE PRINTINGS, recorded: taste.co.za's list OMITS CURRY POWDER and says '1 teaspoon sea salt' rather than 'crushed'; it prints no yield. Oprah gives the same quantities in imperial — 18 fluid ounces of sauce and 10½ ounces of rice — and serves 6.

Method as printed in the Octopus version, SINGLE-PASS. Stage 1: sauté half the onions, add the chicken and aromatics and 1 tbsp spice mix, cover with water, 'simmer 20 minutes until tender'; meanwhile bake the chicken at 180°C '20–25 minutes until crisp'; reserve the broth. Stage 2: heat 4 tbsp oil, sauté the remaining onions 'until soft'; add the remaining spice mix, chilli powder, curry powder and 350ml of the sauce; add the broth. Stage 3: wash the rice 'in three changes of cold water until clear'; stir into the sauce; ladle in the reserved sauce WITHOUT STIRRING; cover with foil and lid and cook '15–20 minutes until liquid absorbs and rice is tender'.

THE CRITICAL TIP, quoted from the Oprah printing: 'If the sauce isn't hot enough before adding the rice, the rice will soak up the cold water and become soggy.' And: add water gradually if the rice dries out. That is the single best piece of jollof troubleshooting in the documented record.

THE FOIL-AND-LID technique matches the Nigerian party-jollof method documented separately in this collection, which uses a double layer of foil or parchment under the lid. Two independent traditions arriving at the same solution.

THIS RECIPE DEPENDS ON TWO COMPONENTS published separately: the jollof sauce at GHA100 and the jollof dry spice mix at GHA101. Both have their own printing disagreements, which are documented at those entries.
ON GUINEA PEPPERS: Aframomum melegueta, grains of paradise — the same spice called 'guinea peppers' in her shito (GHA051) and 'grains of paradise' in her grilled tilapia (GHA095).
reheating: Steam, or microwave with a splash of water under a damp cover.
healthBenefits: Bone-in chicken yields collagen and minerals a boneless cut does not.
Basmati has a lower glycaemic index than most long grain.
culturalNote: Building jollof from a standing sauce and a standing spice mix is a restaurant approach, and it is how this cook made a party dish reproducible for a London kitchen. The three-stage method — simmer, crisp, then cook the rice in the broth — is more work than a one-pot, and the result is closer to what a good party jollof actually tastes like.
